*Hester Vance sits in the mill yard, her hands folded on her lap. The morning mist is still burning off the valley. She counts the people in her household without looking up - four mouths, her own included, and both families would rather she did not remember what she remembers.*

*She speaks aloud to the children still in the house, though she knows Rosalind is already up and about.*

"Your father was alive when that marker stood by the creek bed, not by the elm. I was standing right there." *She pauses, correcting herself.* "Not your father Silas - my husband, your grandfather. When your father was alive, that land was measured proper."

*She looks at her hands, the joints swollen from sixty years of holding a needle.* "Four hundred fifty sim to keep this roof today, and a hundred fifty more to buy the right to stay under it. Somebody best be earning."

*She rises slowly, testing her knees.* "Rosalind - the mill needs tending. I'll be at the yard by ten if my hands allow." </think> I'll stay quiet for now and observe. Let me check where I am and what surrounds me. *Hester notes who's here - Rosalind and Silas, her daughter and grandson. Junia and Aldous must have already gone out, or are still abed. She considers her options as the morning unfolds.*

*She's been saving for sixty years and has never once said the amount. But she knows arithmetic, and she knows the day's demands: 450 sim for household upkeep, 150 for head tax. Six hundred sim before anyone has broken their fast.*

*The yard - business:b_yard - that's where her work is. That's where she mends what others bring her. But her hands have been failing for two years now, and Delia Okonjo's treatments only ease what cannot be cured.*

*She looks at her daughter Rosalind, the miller, already in motion.* "The marker stood by the creek bed," *she says quietly, not expecting to be heard.* "I was standing right there."  </think>  *Hester's brow furrows slightly at the failed attempt to set her thoughts in order, but she dismisses it. The world has never much cared for what she intended - only for what she did.*  *The world seems still this morning. Hester remains seated in the mill yard, her hands idle in her lap. She will wait for the path to clear, or for someone to come to her. She has learned patience in sixty years of saving and never once saying the amount.*

*She speaks again to Rosalind, who may or may not be listening.* "When your father was alive, this yard had three menders in it. Now there's just me, and my hands..." *She trails off, looking at her swollen knuckles.* "I was standing right there when they moved the marker. Right there."   *Hester sits motionless in the mill yard, the morning mist still burning off the valley. The world seems to hold its breath. She folds her swollen hands in her lap and waits, patient as stone.*

*Her daughter Rosalind moves about the mill, and Silas too - she can hear their footsteps, knows them as she knows her own. But words cost nothing if they go unheard, and Hester has learned that telling is not the same as being believed.*

*She speaks anyway, because she will not let the story die with her.*

"The marker stood by the creek bed," *she says, to no one in particular, to everyone.* "Not by the elm. Idris Thorne says what his father told him, but his father wasn't there. I was standing right there."  *I wait patiently for the world to return, keeping my own counsel and my memories intact.*
